title: The ineffability of meaning
subtitle: Why you can't paraphrase a poem
author: Stefan Valdemar Snævarr
introduction: When engaging with poetry, readers will often ask what a particular poem means. The implicit assumption, of course, is that it is possible to reword or paraphrase a poem in a manner which somehow preserves its essence. In this article, philosophy professor Stefan Valdemar Snævarr argues that no such paraphrase is possible. Intrinsic to poetry, Snævarr argues, is a reliance on metaphor, ambiguity, and ineffability which ensures that the only way to grasp the essence of a poem is to read the poem itself.
body:
The New Critics were a school in literary studies that emphasized close reading of literary works, especially poems, and tended to regard such works as autonomous. Poems could be understood as objects, largely independent of the intentions of the poet and the responses of the readers.

The non-paraphrasability of poetry was a central tenet of this school: Summarizing or otherwise retelling poems was considered futile. One of the school’s members Cleanth Brooks coined the phrase “the heresy of paraphrase.” Call it “The Heresy Thesis.”

An undergraduate once asked the darling of the New Critics, Nobel laureate T. S. Eliot, what he meant by the line “lady, three white leopards sat under a juniper tree.” He purportedly replied, “I meant ‘lady, three white leopards sat under a juniper tree.’”

It is said that an undergraduate once asked the darling of the New Critics, Nobel laureate T.S. Eliot, what he meant by the line “lady, three white leopards sat under a juniper tree.” He purportedly replied, “I meant ‘lady, three white leopards sat under a juniper tree.’” The implication, of course, is that the line is not para­phrasable. The New Critic and poet Archibald MacLeish said “A poem should not mean but be” (MacLeish 1964: 1069). Obviously, poems cannot be retold if they only are, but do not mean. They can, however, be meaning­ful and at the same time impossible to paraphrase satisfactorily.

SUGGESTED READING Poetry is philosophy By Magdalena Ostas

Why did Cleanth Brooks think that paraphrase is a heresy? He denied neither that poems could be paraphrased up to a point nor that such a paraphrase can be useful in some contexts. What Brooks did reject was the belief that paraphrase could replace a poem or capture its essence. Moreover, attempts at complete paraphrases of poems need metaphors in order to capture their meaning, but these metaphors in turn stand in need of paraphrase. Certainly, many poems contain propositions, which are easily rephrased, but we must not mistake them for the inner core of these poems. Such propositions are justified in the con­text of the poem as a whole, not in connection with a general paraphrase. Thus, a proposition like John Keats’ “Beauty is truth, truth beauty” gets its precise meaning and significance from its relation to the total context of the poem (Brooks 1968: 157-176).

Brooks was on the right track, but I want to argue in favor of the Heresy Thesis in a somewhat different manner. I shall discriminate between two kinds of paraphrase, the rewording kind and the synopsis type. In the first case, we exchange all or an important part of the words of a poem with other words. In the second case, we make a synopsis of the poem with the aim of capturing its essence.

My first argument in favor of the Heresy Thesis is the following: All aspects of a poem are inseparable: its rhythm, style, sounds, images, emotional flavour, along with its intellectual aspects and the denotations and connotations of its words – even its graphical presen­tation. The whole is bigger than the sum of its parts; a poem is a holis­tic work. If this is the case, then form and content cannot be separated in any clear-cut manner, and so abstracting the content (the message) from the poem by way of synopsis is a risky and none-too-rewarding business. Rewording would not be rewarding, it would be making a new poem.

Further, rhythm often plays a major role in the meaning of a poem, but rhythm can hardly be mirrored by propositions. Hence, it makes no sense to paraphrase rhythm or the contribution it makes to a poem’s meaning.

The second argument is the following: We can often improve upon everyday utterances and aca­demic texts by clarifying them. Indeed, we can clarify texts by rephrasing them and increase our understanding of them by making synopses of them. In contrast, it does not make any sense to suppose we improve upon a poem by clarifying it, either through paraphrase or other means. It is actually an open question whether we can make any changes to a poem without creating a new one.

If the true interpretation of a poem is not possible, then the correct paraphrase is not possible either.

The third argument concerns interpretation: Poems are often ambiguous and the meaning of their various expressions tends to be elusive. Such poems, even all poems, are at least partly a function of various, equally (in)valid interpretations (the meaning of a poem might at least to a certain degree be a sum of such interpretations). This phenomenon of interpretive ambiguity is also present in the famous duck-rabbit figure which can be regarded as either animal with equal validity. This means that the correct paraphrase of most, even all, poems, is relative to interpretations of them. If the true interpretation of a poem is not possible, then the correct paraphrase is not possible either. This holds true for both rewording and synopses.

The fourth argument concerns the purported ineffability of poetry, which might be understood as a function of tacit knowledge or experience. Example of such knowledge can be our knowledge of our friends’ faces, which we cannot express satisfactory in words. So, if aspects of our understanding of certain poems are tacit and cannot be expressed in words, then that might explain our inability to paraphrase them.

The proof is in the pudding – my arguments are not worth much without me giving good examples of a non-paraphrasable poems. I shall try to paraphrase them with the aim of finding out whether a rewording can replace the poem and/or a synopsis capture its essence. I shall use these examples both to support my general arguments and to introduce the fifth argument.

Consider one of the best known poems of the romantic age, the British poet’s William Wordsworth’s (1770-1850) poem "A Slumber did my Spirit Seal":

A slumber did my spirit seal;

I had no human fears:

She seemed a thing that could not feel

The touch of earthly years.

No motion has she now, no force;

She neither hears nor sees:

Rolled round in earth’s diurnal course,

With rocks, and stones, and trees.

What would result from paraphrasing the rhyme and metre in this poem? Is there such a thing as the paraphrasing of rhyme and metre?

What do the first two sentences mean? Do they mean “a short sleep made me forget my woes” or “I was like a somnambulistic person and therefore did not feel the fears ordinary people feel”? From the rest of the poem, we can deduce that the lack of fear concerns a person referred to as “she.” She is called a thing in the third line, which might mean that she is not a human being but some kind of an eternal force. However, in the second stanza it is suggested that she is no longer alive, hence she must have been a living being. But the last two lines are mysterious: Is her body rolling around in the process of earth’s daytime processes? There are so many interpretative possibilities of the various lines of the poem that a synopsis is hardly possible. Of course, any worthwhile synopsis must be a synopsis of the poem as a whole but if some of the lines are difficult, even impossible, to understand, then one cannot make a synopsis which captures its essence.

What about rewording? We cannot exclude the possibility that difficult or even impossible to understand texts might be thus paraphrased. Let me try to reword this poem: “A short sleep dulled my mind, I was not frightened in the human way. The woman seemed an object that could not experience the impact of the human lifespan. She does not move now and is without any energy, neither hearing nor seeing. Her body is in the ground and subject to the forces of the earth, in the same manners slabs, stones, and the woods.”

This uncharming text certainly cannot replace the poem. Wordsworth’s poem’s ineffability gives it a haunting, even terrifying, beauty. My rewording has none of that.

Hermetic, modernist poems are not easier to paraphrase than Wordsworth’s romantic ones – rather the opposite.

Hermetic, modernist poems are not easier to paraphrase than Wordsworth’s romantic ones – rather the opposite. Consider the following poem by the American poet Wallace Stevens:

Valley Candle

My candle burned alone in an immense valley.

Beams of the huge night converged upon it,

Until the wind blew.

Then beams of the huge night

Converged upon its image,

Until the wind blew.

It is hard to see any straightforward way to reword this poem. However, let us try: “My wax light was consumed by its flame, alone in a very big dale. Rays of the immense nighttime met at one point upon it until the wind began to blow. The rays of the immense nighttime met at one point upon its picture until the wind began to blow”.

This way of rewording the poem only results in a depressingly bad “poem,” not capturing the rhythm and density of Stevens’s poem.

What about a synopsis? Again, we have the poetic problem of ambiguity. It might be interpreted as being about the brevity of life where the candle stands for life, the immensity of the valley for eternity, the huge night for the suffering of living beings. The convergences of the beams of that night could be interpreted as standing for the many sources of suffering and the way their combination hurts people. The wind might be death, the image of the candle the memory or heritage of a dead person, which does not mean much, taking into account the suffering that the person has had to endure. Perhaps, there is some way of finding an acceptable paraphrase in light of this interpretation. But other equally valid interpretations are possible and would result in different synopses.

There certainly is no way to paraphrase classical East Asian poetry (Chinese, Japanese, Korean). The reason is that the visual elements of calligraphy are essential parts of these poems. There is no way to make a synopsis of or reword calligraphy, or even put it into words. And pictures cannot be adequately described in words. By implication, the same applies to Kenneth Patchen’s picture-poems where the text is woven into images. Moreover, certain sounds cannot be put into words, hence the sound poems of the Dadaist Hugo Ball cannot be paraphrased (but the critic might deny that they are poems).

Does this mean that there is no way to paraphrase poems? No, there certainly are poems that are at least to a certain degree clearly paraphrasable. Consider this beautiful, untitled micro-poem by the British imagist poet T.E. Hulme:

The flounced edge of a skirt

recoiling like waves off a cliff.

The poem consists of a concrete image, expressed in a clear language, in accordance with the ideas of the imagist school of poetry, a school that flourished in the English-speaking world early in the last century.

It can be reworded thus: “A strip of the fabric of the edge of a skirt is falling back like the ocean waves in the vicinity of a cliff.” Well, this rewording lacks the elegance of the poem and can be called “another poem, a very bad one”. However, the poem is not very hard to understand, the following synopsis makes sense: The poem describes a strip of fabric of a skirt, moving like ocean waves near a cliff.

The problem is that its main meaning might lie in what is not said. The speaking voice in the poem might be experiencing the skirt’s edge as symbolic of the qualities of the lady, clad in that garment. Thus, there might after all be an ineffable side to this apparently simple poem.

Notice that Hulme’s poem could easily be a sentence in a prose work. The trouble is that if all poems were like that and were at least to a certain degree para­phrasable, then there would hardly be any clear difference between poems and prose. Poetry might become an accessory to prose or even disappear entirely (I just assume that prose is by and large easier to paraphrase than poetry – after all, we can at least recount the plot of most novels in a fairly objective way). So, being usually non-paraphrasable or difficult to paraphrase might be necessary for the existence of poetry. A proto-typical poem is not paraphrasable.

This is my fifth and final argument in favor of the Heresy Thesis. The conclusion of these arguments is that even though some poems might be partly para­phrasable, it must be the rule, not the exception, that they are not.

Now, a critic might ask whether the problem with my attempts in this article at paraphrasing poems is not that their lack of paraphrasability but rather my own shortcomings. Perhaps someone else could do the job of paraphrasing these poems successfully.

My rejoinder is simply that the onus is on the critic.

Let me end this article with a quote from Tristan Tzara’s dadaist poem "Chronicle":

“phrase paraphrase antiphrase parachute paraphrase...”

Can anybody please   paraphrase this line?
